subject: Social Sciences

sources.title: NZC Social Sciences Years 0–10, September 2026

topics.name: Roles in a community
topics.description: People in a community can take different roles and cooperate to meet shared needs.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 9, Phase 1 > Civics and Society; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Describe how staff, visitors and volunteers can have different roles in a community service.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Staff organise and support the service; visitors use it; volunteers may help with agreed tasks.
misconceptions: Everyone in a community must have the same role.
topics.question: A library has staff, visitors and volunteers. How might their roles differ?
topics.answer: Staff organise and support the service; visitors use it; volunteers may help with agreed tasks.
topics.explanation: People in a community can take different roles and cooperate to meet shared needs.
hints: Who looks after the books?
Who comes to borrow them?
topics.activity: Choose a familiar community place and draw two roles and how they help it function.

topics.name: Belonging to groups
topics.description: A person may belong to several different groups, and people express belonging in varied ways.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 9, Phase 1 > Civics and Society; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Recognise that a person can belong to more than one group.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Yes. People may belong to several groups at the same time.
misconceptions: A person can belong to only one community.
topics.question: Can someone belong to both a sports team and a family group?
topics.answer: Yes. People may belong to several groups at the same time.
topics.explanation: A person may belong to several different groups, and people express belonging in varied ways.
hints: How many groups can a person take part in?
Think about groups with different purposes.
topics.activity: Create a fictional person and name two groups they belong to and one activity each group shares.

topics.name: Everyday life in the past and present
topics.description: People's experiences can show both continuity and change over time. A source provides evidence about a particular time and place.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 10–12, Phase 1 > History; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain what a historical photograph can show and what it cannot establish alone.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: It shows what is visible in that moment, but it cannot by itself tell you every child's experience.
misconceptions: One photograph tells the whole story of everyone in the past.
topics.question: An older photograph shows children walking to school. What can it tell you, and what can it not tell you?
topics.answer: It shows what is visible in that moment, but it cannot by itself tell you every child's experience.
topics.explanation: People's experiences can show both continuity and change over time. A source provides evidence about a particular time and place.
hints: What is visible in the photograph?
What information lies outside the picture?
topics.activity: Compare two attributed pictures of school life and identify one similarity, one difference and one question.

topics.name: Objects as evidence of the past
topics.description: An object can provide clues about earlier lives, but a historian needs context and other sources to understand how it was used.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 10–12, Phase 1 > History; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Ask a question that could help establish who used an object and when.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: For example, “Who used it, and when?”
misconceptions: An object's appearance alone proves its complete history.
topics.question: An old lunchbox is found in a collection. What question could help explain its past use?
topics.answer: For example, “Who used it, and when?”
topics.explanation: An object can provide clues about earlier lives, but a historian needs context and other sources to understand how it was used.
hints: What information is missing from the object alone?
Ask about a person, place or time.
topics.activity: Examine a picture of a historical object and list two observations and one question for its curator.

topics.name: Features of places
topics.description: A place can be described by its location and visible natural and human-made features. People can have different connections to the same place.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 13–14, Phase 1 > Geography; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Distinguish a natural feature from a human-made feature of a place.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: For example, sand dunes are natural and a walkway is human-made.
misconceptions: Every feature of a place was made by people.
topics.question: Name one natural and one human-made feature that might appear near a beach.
topics.answer: For example, sand dunes are natural and a walkway is human-made.
topics.explanation: A place can be described by its location and visible natural and human-made features. People can have different connections to the same place.
hints: Which feature was made by people?
Which feature occurs in the environment?
topics.activity: Draw a familiar or fictional place and label a natural feature and a human-made feature.

topics.name: Maps and location
topics.description: A map represents places and uses symbols or labels to help a reader locate features.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 13–14, Phase 1 > Geography; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Use a map key to identify where a symbol indicates a place.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: It helps locate a park on the map.
misconceptions: Map symbols always explain themselves without a key or labels.
topics.question: A map key shows a tree symbol for a park. What does that symbol help the reader find?
topics.answer: It helps locate a park on the map.
topics.explanation: A map represents places and uses symbols or labels to help a reader locate features.
hints: Check what the key says.
Find the matching symbol on the map.
topics.activity: Make a simple map of an imaginary neighbourhood with a key for three features.

topics.name: Money and everyday choices
topics.description: People make choices about how to use limited money for different needs and wants.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 15, Phase 1 > Financial and Economic Activity; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Calculate the money remaining after a stated purchase.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: $2 remains.
misconceptions: Spending money does not change the amount available for later choices.
topics.question: A person has $5 and chooses a $3 lunch. How much remains?
topics.answer: $2 remains.
topics.explanation: People make choices about how to use limited money for different needs and wants.
hints: Subtract the lunch price from the starting amount.
Five minus three is two.
topics.activity: Use invented prices to choose between two items and calculate what would remain from a small budget.

topics.name: Goods and services
topics.description: A good is an item people can obtain; a service is an activity provided for someone.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 15, Phase 1 > Financial and Economic Activity; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Classify a haircut as a service rather than a good.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: It is a service because someone provides an activity.
misconceptions: Every purchase is a physical object.
topics.question: Is a haircut a good or a service?
topics.answer: It is a service because someone provides an activity.
topics.explanation: A good is an item people can obtain; a service is an activity provided for someone.
hints: Is the main thing an object or an action?
What is the hairdresser doing?
topics.activity: Sort picture cards of everyday goods and services, explaining two choices.

topics.name: Rules, values and fairness
topics.description: Groups create rules to support shared purposes and values; people can discuss whether a rule works fairly.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 17–18, Phase 2 > Civics and Society; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Ask whether a proposed rule gives people a reasonable opportunity to participate.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: For example, “Does everyone have a reasonable opportunity to participate?”
misconceptions: A rule is automatically fair simply because it exists.
topics.question: A class rule gives only one person a turn. What question could help assess its fairness?
topics.answer: For example, “Does everyone have a reasonable opportunity to participate?”
topics.explanation: Groups create rules to support shared purposes and values; people can discuss whether a rule works fairly.
hints: Who is affected by the rule?
Would different people have a chance to take part?
topics.activity: Discuss a fictional group rule, who it affects and one way to improve it.

topics.name: Voting and having a voice
topics.description: In a democracy, participation can include expressing views and voting in elections. Group decision-making also involves respecting others' rights.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 17–18, Phase 2 > Civics and Society; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain why listening to different views can inform a group vote.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: It helps members understand options and consider how different people may be affected.
misconceptions: Democracy means people are never allowed to disagree.
topics.question: Why might a group hear different views before voting on a proposal?
topics.answer: It helps members understand options and consider how different people may be affected.
topics.explanation: In a democracy, participation can include expressing views and voting in elections. Group decision-making also involves respecting others' rights.
hints: What information could different people contribute?
How could it help before a decision?
topics.activity: Use a fictional class decision to practise giving reasons, listening and voting without requiring personal political views.

topics.name: Voyaging and migration
topics.description: People have moved and voyaged for different reasons. Their journeys and settlement can change communities and environments.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 19–24, Phase 2 > History; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Ask a question comparing the reasons or challenges of historical journeys.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: For example, “Why did the people travel, and what challenges did they face?”
misconceptions: All people moved for exactly the same reason.
topics.question: What question could help compare two historical journeys?
topics.answer: For example, “Why did the people travel, and what challenges did they face?”
topics.explanation: People have moved and voyaged for different reasons. Their journeys and settlement can change communities and environments.
hints: Consider both the reason and the experience.
What might have been difficult during the journey?
topics.activity: Compare two attributed accounts of migration and record a reason, a challenge and a change for each.

topics.name: Continuity and change in communities
topics.description: Historical change can affect how people live, while some practices and connections continue over time.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 19–24, Phase 2 > History; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Identify something that can continue when a community's transport changes.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: People may still travel or trade, even though the transport method changes.
misconceptions: When one feature changes, every aspect of life must change too.
topics.question: If a town's transport changes from boats to roads, what might stay the same?
topics.answer: People may still travel or trade, even though the transport method changes.
topics.explanation: Historical change can affect how people live, while some practices and connections continue over time.
hints: Separate the purpose from the method.
What need might the transport still meet?
topics.activity: Create a timeline for a fictional town showing one change and one continuity; distinguish it from real local history.

topics.name: Landforms and processes
topics.description: Landscapes are shaped by processes such as erosion and deposition, and features of a place can influence how people use it.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 25–26, Phase 2 > Geography; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain how flowing water can erode and carry material in a river valley.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: It can erode material and carry sediment, changing landforms over time.
misconceptions: Landforms never change after they first appear.
topics.question: How can flowing water contribute to shaping a river valley?
topics.answer: It can erode material and carry sediment, changing landforms over time.
topics.explanation: Landscapes are shaped by processes such as erosion and deposition, and features of a place can influence how people use it.
hints: What can moving water pick up?
What happens to the landscape when material is removed or deposited?
topics.activity: Use a labelled diagram to trace sediment movement along a fictional stream and discuss a possible effect on people.

topics.name: Scale and geographic comparison
topics.description: Maps and images can show places at different scales, from a local street to a region or the world. Each scale reveals different details.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 25–26, Phase 2 > Geography; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Compare the detail shown on neighbourhood and world maps.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: A neighbourhood map, because it shows a smaller area in more detail.
misconceptions: Every map shows the same level of detail.
topics.question: Would a neighbourhood map or a world map usually show individual streets more clearly?
topics.answer: A neighbourhood map, because it shows a smaller area in more detail.
topics.explanation: Maps and images can show places at different scales, from a local street to a region or the world. Each scale reveals different details.
hints: Which map covers the smaller area?
Which can show finer local detail?
topics.activity: Compare a local map and a national map, noting one useful feature visible at each scale.

topics.name: Saving towards a goal
topics.description: A savings plan connects a goal, an amount and a timeframe. Unexpected changes can require a plan to be revised.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 27–28, Phase 2 > Financial and Economic Activity; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Calculate the time needed to reach a fictional savings goal at a fixed weekly amount.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Four weeks, assuming no changes.
misconceptions: A savings goal does not depend on the amount saved.
topics.question: A fictional goal costs $20 and $5 is saved each week. How many weeks are needed?
topics.answer: Four weeks, assuming no changes.
topics.explanation: A savings plan connects a goal, an amount and a timeframe. Unexpected changes can require a plan to be revised.
hints: Divide the total goal by the weekly amount.
How many groups of five make twenty?
topics.activity: Plan for an invented purchase using simple weekly savings and explain one reason the plan might change.

topics.name: Introducing interest
topics.description: Interest is an amount associated with saving or borrowing money. Its effect depends on the agreement and the time involved.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 27–28, Phase 2 > Financial and Economic Activity; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Calculate a savings balance after a stated amount of interest is added.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: $105.
misconceptions: Interest always reduces a savings balance.
topics.question: If $100 earns $5 interest over a stated period, how much is in the account before any other changes?
topics.explanation: Interest is an amount associated with saving or borrowing money. Its effect depends on the agreement and the time involved.
hints: Add the interest to the original amount.
One hundred plus five is 105.
topics.activity: Use fictional amounts to compare a savings balance before and after one stated interest payment.

topics.name: Local decisions and participation
topics.description: Local government makes decisions affecting communities. People can participate by seeking information and sharing views through available processes.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 30–31, Phase 3 > Civics and Society; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Identify a way residents can take part in consultation on a local proposal.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: They could read the proposal and provide feedback through an available consultation process.
misconceptions: Only elected officials can have any input into local decisions.
topics.question: A council proposes changing a local park. What is one way residents could participate?
topics.answer: They could read the proposal and provide feedback through an available consultation process.
topics.explanation: Local government makes decisions affecting communities. People can participate by seeking information and sharing views through available processes.
hints: Who is proposing the change?
How might people share views before a decision?
topics.activity: Review a fictional council proposal and prepare one question and one respectful piece of feedback.

topics.name: Respectful democratic dialogue
topics.description: People can disagree about values or proposals while listening to reasons, checking claims and discussing differences peacefully.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 30–31, Phase 3 > Civics and Society; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Respond constructively to disagreement by listening and asking a relevant question.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Summarise the other person's concern and ask a relevant question before giving a reasoned view.
misconceptions: Respectful discussion requires everyone to hold the same opinion.
topics.question: Two people disagree about a cycle path. What response could keep the discussion constructive?
topics.answer: Summarise the other person's concern and ask a relevant question before giving a reasoned view.
topics.explanation: People can disagree about values or proposals while listening to reasons, checking claims and discussing differences peacefully.
hints: First show what you heard.
Then ask a question about the idea.
topics.activity: Role-play two fictional viewpoints on a community proposal, using evidence and respectful follow-up questions.

topics.name: Cultural contact and consequences
topics.description: Contact between groups can involve exchanges of ideas, goods and technologies as well as conflict and unequal consequences.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 32–34, Phase 3 > History; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain why accounts from different groups can reveal different experiences of contact.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Different groups may experience and describe the same event differently.
misconceptions: All groups experience cultural contact in the same way.
topics.question: Why should a historian consider more than one group's account of a contact event?
topics.answer: Different groups may experience and describe the same event differently.
topics.explanation: Contact between groups can involve exchanges of ideas, goods and technologies as well as conflict and unequal consequences.
hints: Whose experiences might differ?
What might a second account reveal?
topics.activity: Compare two attributed historical perspectives and note a shared event and a difference in experience.

topics.name: Te Tiriti o Waitangi and historical sources
topics.description: Te Tiriti o Waitangi and the Treaty of Waitangi are central to New Zealand history. Historical sources and the differences between texts and interpretations should be examined with appropriate Māori and other perspectives.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 32–34, Phase 3 > History; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain why comparing the Māori and English treaty texts can inform historical interpretation.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: The texts differ, and comparing them alongside reliable interpretations helps explain differing understandings and consequences.
misconceptions: The different texts and perspectives can be understood fully from an unsupported summary.
topics.question: Why is it useful to consult both te reo Māori and English texts when studying Te Tiriti and the Treaty?
topics.answer: The texts differ, and comparing them alongside reliable interpretations helps explain differing understandings and consequences.
topics.explanation: Te Tiriti o Waitangi and the Treaty of Waitangi are central to New Zealand history. Historical sources and the differences between texts and interpretations should be examined with appropriate Māori and other perspectives.
hints: How many texts are being considered?
Can different wording affect interpretation?
topics.activity: Use a trusted public source to compare a short attributed explanation of the texts, then record one question for further inquiry.

topics.name: Migration and places
topics.description: Migration can change the places people leave and enter, affecting people, communities and environments in different ways.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 35–36, Phase 3 > Geography; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Ask a question about how migration may affect a town's housing, services or employment.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: For example, “How did demand for housing, services or employment change?”
misconceptions: Migration affects every place in exactly the same way.
topics.question: What is one question to ask about the effect of migration on a town?
topics.answer: For example, “How did demand for housing, services or employment change?”
topics.explanation: Migration can change the places people leave and enter, affecting people, communities and environments in different ways.
hints: What might more or fewer residents need?
How could this affect local services?
topics.activity: Use a fictional population chart to describe a change and suggest two questions about its local effects.

topics.name: Natural processes and communities
topics.description: Natural processes can become hazards when people, buildings or infrastructure are exposed to them. Impacts depend on both the process and vulnerability.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 35–36, Phase 3 > Geography; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain how exposure and local conditions influence the impacts of heavy rain.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Differences in exposure, drainage, land use and preparedness can change the impact.
misconceptions: A natural event has identical impacts everywhere.
topics.question: Why can the same heavy rain have different effects in two places?
topics.answer: Differences in exposure, drainage, land use and preparedness can change the impact.
topics.explanation: Natural processes can become hazards when people, buildings or infrastructure are exposed to them. Impacts depend on both the process and vulnerability.
hints: Compare the places, not just the rainfall.
What could affect where water collects?
topics.activity: Compare two fictional flood maps and identify a feature that could affect each community's exposure.

topics.name: Planning a shared budget
topics.description: A group budget requires shared goals, an estimate of resources and decisions about competing uses.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 37–38, Phase 3 > Financial and Economic Activity; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Calculate a group's remaining budget after a stated expense.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: $18.
misconceptions: A shared budget does not need agreement about priorities.
topics.question: A fictional group has $30 for an event and spends $12 on materials. How much is left?
topics.explanation: A group budget requires shared goals, an estimate of resources and decisions about competing uses.
hints: Subtract the materials cost from the total.
Thirty minus twelve is eighteen.
topics.activity: Plan a small fictional event using invented prices, then explain how the group might choose between two remaining costs.

topics.name: Recognising possible scams
topics.description: Financial decisions involve checking information and recognising possible scams. An unexpected request for payment or private information deserves verification through a trusted independent channel.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 37–38, Phase 3 > Financial and Economic Activity; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Identify a safer response to an unexpected request for a bank password.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Do not share the password; check the claim independently through a trusted official contact and seek help if needed.
misconceptions: Urgency alone proves that a financial message is trustworthy.
topics.question: A message says an unknown sender needs your bank password urgently. What is a safer response?
topics.answer: Do not share the password; check the claim independently through a trusted official contact and seek help if needed.
topics.explanation: Financial decisions involve checking information and recognising possible scams. An unexpected request for payment or private information deserves verification through a trusted independent channel.
hints: Does a legitimate password need to be shared with a stranger?
Can you verify the message without using its link?
topics.activity: Inspect a fictional message and underline two warning signs; use made-up details only.

topics.name: Representative democracy
topics.description: In a representative democracy, elected representatives participate in decision-making on behalf of communities, and people have different ways to engage with public issues.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 40–41, Phase 4 > Civics and Society; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Identify a way to influence a public issue between elections.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: For example, they can contact a representative, make a submission or take part in a lawful public discussion.
misconceptions: Democratic participation happens only on election day.
topics.question: How can a citizen influence an issue between elections?
topics.answer: For example, they can contact a representative, make a submission or take part in a lawful public discussion.
topics.explanation: In a representative democracy, elected representatives participate in decision-making on behalf of communities, and people have different ways to engage with public issues.
hints: Participation can happen outside election day.
Consider ways to communicate a view to decision-makers.
topics.activity: Choose a fictional public issue and compare two possible ways of participating.

topics.name: International cooperation
topics.description: Countries can use agreements and institutions to cooperate on shared challenges, although their interests and perspectives may differ.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 40–41, Phase 4 > Civics and Society; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain why countries may coordinate their responses to a cross-border problem.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: A shared response can coordinate information and actions when no single country can address the issue alone.
misconceptions: Countries always have identical interests when they cooperate.
topics.question: Why might countries cooperate on a problem that crosses borders?
topics.answer: A shared response can coordinate information and actions when no single country can address the issue alone.
topics.explanation: Countries can use agreements and institutions to cooperate on shared challenges, although their interests and perspectives may differ.
hints: Does the problem stop at one border?
What could coordinated action add?
topics.activity: Choose a fictional shared environmental challenge and propose one cooperative action and one possible disagreement.

topics.name: Multiple causes and consequences
topics.description: Historical events can have interconnected causes and short- and long-term consequences. Explanations should use evidence and distinguish perspectives.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 42–47, Phase 4 > History; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain how several factors can contribute to a historical conflict.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Political, economic, social or other factors can interact; evidence is needed to explain their roles.
misconceptions: A complex conflict must have exactly one cause.
topics.question: Why might a conflict have more than one cause?
topics.answer: Political, economic, social or other factors can interact; evidence is needed to explain their roles.
topics.explanation: Historical events can have interconnected causes and short- and long-term consequences. Explanations should use evidence and distinguish perspectives.
hints: Think of more than one kind of pressure.
Could these factors influence each other?
topics.activity: Build an evidence-based cause-and-consequence diagram for an attributed historical case, noting uncertainty.

topics.name: Comparing historical interpretations
topics.description: Historians interpret evidence from different sources and may reach differing conclusions. Context, authorship and missing voices affect interpretation.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 42–47, Phase 4 > History; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Compare the creators, purposes and evidence of conflicting historical accounts.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Consider who created each account, when, for what purpose and what evidence or perspectives are missing.
misconceptions: A historical account is complete and neutral simply because it is old.
topics.question: Two accounts disagree about an event. What should a reader examine?
topics.answer: Consider who created each account, when, for what purpose and what evidence or perspectives are missing.
topics.explanation: Historians interpret evidence from different sources and may reach differing conclusions. Context, authorship and missing voices affect interpretation.
hints: Who created each source?
What might each author know or leave out?
topics.activity: Compare two attributed accounts of a historical event and describe one point of agreement, one difference and one source limitation.

topics.name: Tourism and sustainability
topics.description: Tourism can bring opportunities and place pressure on communities and environments. Sustainable decisions consider effects and trade-offs over time.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 48–50, Phase 4 > Geography; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Identify a possible benefit and pressure from increased tourism.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Visitors may support local activity while increasing pressure on infrastructure or ecosystems.
misconceptions: Tourism has only positive effects or only negative effects everywhere.
topics.question: Why might more visitors create both benefits and challenges for a destination?
topics.answer: Visitors may support local activity while increasing pressure on infrastructure or ecosystems.
topics.explanation: Tourism can bring opportunities and place pressure on communities and environments. Sustainable decisions consider effects and trade-offs over time.
hints: Think about an economic benefit.
What might happen to services or the environment?
topics.activity: Use a fictional visitor scenario to list a benefit, a pressure and one possible response.

topics.name: Urban growth and environments
topics.description: Urbanisation changes where people live and can affect housing, transport, services and ecosystems. Effects depend on local planning and context.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 48–50, Phase 4 > Geography; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain how rapid population growth can increase demand for urban services.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: More people may need housing, transport, water and other services faster than capacity expands.
misconceptions: Growing cities face no choices about land or infrastructure.
topics.question: How could rapid population growth put pressure on a city's services?
topics.answer: More people may need housing, transport, water and other services faster than capacity expands.
topics.explanation: Urbanisation changes where people live and can affect housing, transport, services and ecosystems. Effects depend on local planning and context.
hints: Which services do residents use?
What happens if demand grows faster than supply?
topics.activity: Interpret a fictional city population graph and discuss two questions for sustainable planning.

topics.name: Financial risk and return
topics.description: Financial choices can involve uncertainty. Comparing potential returns, costs, timeframes and risks can help people understand trade-offs.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 51–52, Phase 4 > Financial and Economic Activity; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Identify why a promise of high return with no risk deserves scrutiny.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: All financial offers need evidence and scrutiny; unusually certain promises may be a warning sign.
misconceptions: A high promised return guarantees a safe outcome.
topics.question: Why is an offer promising a high return with no risk worth investigating carefully?
topics.answer: All financial offers need evidence and scrutiny; unusually certain promises may be a warning sign.
topics.explanation: Financial choices can involve uncertainty. Comparing potential returns, costs, timeframes and risks can help people understand trade-offs.
hints: What information supports the promise?
Could any financial outcome be uncertain?
topics.activity: Compare two invented savings or investment descriptions and list questions about fees, risk and timeframe.

topics.name: Borrowing and long-term budgets
topics.description: Borrowing creates an obligation to repay, often with costs. A budget can help compare repayments with other financial commitments.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 51–52, Phase 4 > Financial and Economic Activity; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain why a borrower should compare the total repayment with the amount borrowed.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Interest and fees can make the total amount repaid larger than the amount initially borrowed.
misconceptions: Borrowing always costs exactly the amount received.
topics.question: Why should someone consider total repayment as well as the amount borrowed?
topics.answer: Interest and fees can make the total amount repaid larger than the amount initially borrowed.
topics.explanation: Borrowing creates an obligation to repay, often with costs. A budget can help compare repayments with other financial commitments.
hints: What might be added to the amount borrowed?
Compare the total paid with the amount received.
topics.activity: Use a fictional interest-free example and a separate example with a clearly stated fee to compare total repayments.

topics.name: Remembering people and events

objectives: Explain why direct barter requires both parties to accept the proposed exchange.
evidence: Explains one limitation of swapping goods directly.
misconceptions: Barter works equally well even when neither person wants what the other offers.
topics.question: Why might swapping bread directly for a haircut be difficult?
topics.answer: The baker and the hairdresser both need to want what the other offers.
topics.explanation: A direct exchange depends on each party accepting what the other offers; money can make exchanges more flexible.
hints: What must each person want?
Both need to agree to the swap.
topics.activity: Use fictional offer cards to find a swap both participants would accept, then discuss why another swap did not work.

topics.name: Paid work and volunteering
topics.description: People contribute work in different ways: some work is paid, while other work helps people without earning wages.
topics.locator: PDF p. 27, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Financial and Economic Activity > Year 4 knowledge
objectives: Give an example of unpaid work that benefits a community.
evidence: Gives a specific example of work that helps a community without wages.
misconceptions: Work only counts as useful if someone is paid for it.
topics.question: Can a person contribute useful work without earning wages?
topics.answer: Yes. For example, a volunteer can help in a community garden without wages.
topics.explanation: Work can support other people or a community even when it does not produce income for the worker.
hints: Think about people who choose to help a community.
Volunteering is one example.
topics.activity: List one fictional paid role and one volunteer role and describe how each helps others.

topics.name: Comparing value for money
topics.description: Comparing unit prices, quality and suitability can help people judge value when money is limited.
topics.locator: PDF p. 28, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Financial and Economic Activity > Year 5 knowledge
objectives: Compare the cost per equal quantity of two fictional offers.
evidence: Compares the cost per equal quantity in two fictional offers.
misconceptions: The bigger packet is automatically the better value regardless of price or suitability.
topics.question: Two equal-quality drinks cost $2 for 200 mL and $3 for 400 mL. Which costs less per 100 mL?
topics.answer: The 400 mL drink costs less per 100 mL: $0.75 compared with $1.
topics.explanation: Divide each price by the number of 100 mL portions; suitability and whether the whole amount is needed still matter.
hints: How many 100 mL portions are in each drink?
Divide $2 by two and $3 by four.
topics.activity: Compare two fictional offers using unit price, whether the amount is needed and a stated quality.

topics.name: Interest for savers and borrowers
topics.description: Interest can be money paid to a saver or a cost paid by a borrower, depending on the agreement.
topics.locator: PDF p. 27, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Financial and Economic Activity > Year 6 knowledge
objectives: Distinguish interest paid by a borrower from interest a saver may receive.
evidence: Distinguishes who receives and who pays interest in a simple savings or borrowing example.
misconceptions: Interest always means extra money received by the borrower.
topics.question: In a typical loan, who pays interest: the borrower or the lender?
topics.answer: The borrower pays interest to the lender.
topics.explanation: Interest is a cost of borrowing; in a savings arrangement a saver may receive interest instead.
hints: Who is using someone else's money?
The borrower usually pays for the loan.
topics.activity: Make a two-column diagram showing the direction of interest for a fictional savings account and a loan.

topics.name: Keeping financial information private
topics.description: Protecting passwords and personal financial details is part of managing money safely.
topics.locator: PDF p. 28, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Financial and Economic Activity > Year 6 knowledge
objectives: Identify a bank password as private financial information.
evidence: Identifies a password as private and a shop's public price as shareable.
misconceptions: A message can be trusted with a password if it says it is urgent.
topics.question: Which should stay private: a bank password or the public price of a book?
topics.answer: A bank password should stay private.
topics.explanation: Passwords can provide access to an account; a public price is intended to be shared.
hints: Which detail could allow someone to access an account?
Keep passwords private.
topics.activity: Sort fictional information cards into private details and public information; do not share any real passwords.

topics.name: Currency exchange
topics.description: Different countries use different currencies, and an exchange rate describes how much of one currency can be exchanged for another.
topics.locator: PDF p. 37, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Financial and Economic Activity > Year 7 knowledge
objectives: Calculate a fictional currency exchange using a stated rate before fees.
evidence: Calculates a fictional exchange before fees and recognises that actual rates change.
misconceptions: Currencies always exchange one-for-one and the rate never changes.
topics.question: At a fictional rate of 1 NZ dollar to 2 units, how many units would 10 NZ dollars buy before fees?
topics.answer: 20 units.
topics.explanation: Multiply 10 by 2; real exchange rates and provider fees vary.
hints: Each dollar buys two units in this fictional example.
Multiply 10 by 2.
topics.activity: Use made-up exchange-rate cards to compare two conversions, clearly marking that the rates are not current quotes.

topics.name: Group priorities and trade-offs
topics.description: A group with limited money can compare priorities and give reasons for choosing one use over another.
topics.locator: PDF p. 37, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Financial and Economic Activity > Year 7 practices
objectives: Identify the option a group gives up when it chooses another use for limited money.
evidence: Explains what is given up when a group makes a financial choice.
misconceptions: A budget lets a group buy every desirable option without a trade-off.
topics.question: A group can afford either a shelter or new sports gear, but not both. What trade-off does choosing the shelter involve?
topics.answer: The group gives up buying the sports gear with that money.
topics.explanation: Limited resources mean using money for one priority leaves less available for another.
hints: The budget covers only one option.
Which option is not purchased?
topics.activity: Give a fictional group a fixed budget and ask members to explain two priorities before agreeing on a choice.

topics.name: Advertising and purchasing decisions
topics.description: Advertising can influence decisions through urgency, endorsements and selective claims; buyers can pause to check details.
topics.locator: PDF p. 37, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Financial and Economic Activity > Year 8 knowledge
objectives: Recognise an urgency claim and suggest checks before making a purchase.
evidence: Identifies an urgency claim as a reason to check rather than rush.
misconceptions: A countdown in an advertisement proves an offer is the best available.
topics.question: An advertisement says a product must be bought in five minutes. What is a sensible next step?
topics.answer: Pause and independently check the product, total price and conditions.
topics.explanation: Urgency can pressure a decision; comparing reliable information makes the choice more informed.
hints: Does the message give you time to compare?
A countdown is a reason to check rather than rush.
topics.activity: Annotate a fictional advertisement, underline its persuasive claims and list what needs independent checking.

topics.name: Economic sectors
topics.description: Economic activity can include obtaining raw materials, making products and providing services.
topics.locator: PDF p. 51, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Financial and Economic Activity > Year 9 knowledge
objectives: Classify processing logs into boards as secondary-sector activity.
evidence: Classifies a stated example as primary, secondary or tertiary activity.
misconceptions: All economic activity consists of selling imported goods.
topics.question: A sawmill turns logs into timber boards. Which sector is this: primary, secondary or tertiary?
topics.answer: The secondary sector.
topics.explanation: Manufacturing or processing raw materials into products belongs to the secondary sector.
hints: The logs are being processed into a new product.
Processing belongs to the secondary sector.
topics.activity: Sort fictional examples of farming, manufacturing and transport into three sector columns.

topics.name: Compounding on debt
topics.description: If interest is added to a debt, later interest can be calculated on the increased balance as well as the original amount.
topics.locator: PDF p. 52, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Financial and Economic Activity > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Calculate a fictional debt balance after two periods of compounding.
evidence: Calculates a simple two-period example with stated interest and no repayments or fees.
misconceptions: Interest is always calculated only on the original amount, even when unpaid interest is added to the debt.
topics.question: A $100 debt grows by 10% per year for two years with no payments or fees. What is the balance?
topics.explanation: After one year it is $110; another 10% of $110 adds $11, giving $121.
hints: Calculate 10% of the first year's balance, not just the original $100.
The balance goes from $100 to $110, then to $121.
topics.activity: Make a two-year table for a fictional debt, showing opening balance, interest and closing balance each year.

topics.name: Reading employment terms
topics.description: Employment agreements can differ in hours, pay, leave and notice, affecting income and planning.
topics.locator: PDF p. 52, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Financial and Economic Activity > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Identify pay, hours, leave or notice terms to check in fictional agreements.
evidence: Identifies specific terms to check in a fictional employment agreement.
misconceptions: Every job has identical hours and leave conditions.
topics.question: Name two terms to check when comparing fictional employment agreements.
topics.answer: Check terms such as hours and pay, or leave and notice.
topics.explanation: The conditions affect how much someone may earn and what commitments or entitlements apply.
hints: Look for when and how much the person works.
Hours and pay are two useful terms.
topics.activity: Highlight hours, pay, leave and notice in two fictional agreements; do not share private employment information.

topics.name: Australia's varied landscapes
topics.description: Australia contains varied physical landscapes, including deserts, mountain ranges and coral reefs.
topics.locator: PDF p. 25, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Geography > Year 4 knowledge
objectives: Identify contrasting physical landscapes found in Australia.
evidence: Identifies two distinct physical features of Australia.
misconceptions: All of Australia's landscape is desert.
topics.question: Name two different types of Australian physical landscape.
topics.answer: Examples include interior deserts and the Great Dividing Range, or a coral reef.
topics.explanation: Australia's large area includes different landforms and environments rather than a single landscape type.
hints: Think of mountains as well as deserts.
A mountain range and a reef are other examples.
topics.activity: On a labelled map, find the Great Dividing Range, one interior desert and the Great Barrier Reef.

topics.name: Settlement site and situation
topics.description: A settlement's site is its physical location and features; its situation describes its position and connections relative to other places.
topics.locator: PDF p. 26, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Geography > Year 4 knowledge
objectives: Distinguish a settlement's physical site features from its connections to other places.
evidence: Distinguishes a harbour as a site feature from a road connection as part of situation.
misconceptions: A settlement's physical features and its connections to other places mean exactly the same thing.
topics.question: Is a natural harbour a feature of a settlement's site or its situation?
topics.answer: It is a site feature.
topics.explanation: A natural harbour is a physical feature of the place itself; connections to other places describe situation.
hints: Is the harbour at the place or a link to another place?
A physical feature at the place is part of its site.
topics.activity: Mark a harbour at a fictional town and a road to another town, then label site and situation.

topics.name: Reading a landform cross-section
topics.description: A cross-section represents the side profile of land between two points and shows changes in height.
topics.locator: PDF p. 25, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Geography > Year 5 knowledge
objectives: Compare heights on a side-profile drawing of a landscape.
evidence: Uses a side-profile diagram to identify the higher of two points.
misconceptions: A cross-section only shows the distance between points and cannot show height.
topics.question: On a side-profile drawing, point A is at 100 metres and point B is at 300 metres. Which is higher?
topics.answer: Point B is higher.
topics.explanation: The vertical measurements show B is 200 metres above A in this example.
hints: Compare 100 m and 300 m.
The larger height is B.
topics.activity: Draw a side profile with a river valley and a hill, then mark and compare two heights.

topics.name: Investigating a local landform
topics.description: A local landform can be investigated through observations, maps, dated images and accounts from people connected with the place.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 25–26, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Geography > Year 5 knowledge and practices
objectives: Suggest dated evidence and appropriate local accounts for investigating landform change.
evidence: Suggests a way to compare evidence of change while respecting community-held knowledge.
misconceptions: A single invented story is enough to establish the history and significance of a local landform.
topics.question: How could learners investigate whether a local riverbank has changed over time?
topics.answer: Compare dated maps or photographs and seek appropriate local accounts from people connected with the place.
topics.explanation: Different dated evidence can show change, while local people may hold knowledge and perspectives that require permission and respect.
hints: Look for evidence made at different times.
Use dated images and ask rather than invent local histories.
topics.activity: Compare two teacher-provided images of a local landform and list changes and questions; use iwi or hapū sources where they are publicly shared.
materials: two dated local images or maps

topics.name: Rainforest change and communities
topics.description: Deforestation can affect habitats, soil and communities that depend on a rainforest, with effects varying by place.
topics.locator: PDF p. 26, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Geography > Year 6 knowledge
objectives: Identify a possible environmental or community consequence of rainforest clearance.
evidence: Identifies an environmental or social consequence of clearing forest.
misconceptions: Removing rainforest cannot affect people living in or near it.
topics.question: What is one possible effect of large-scale rainforest clearance?
topics.answer: It can reduce habitat, increase soil erosion or disrupt communities that depend on the forest.
topics.explanation: Trees, soil, water and communities are connected, so removing forest can affect more than the trees themselves.
hints: Think about organisms and people that use the forest.
Habitat loss is one possible effect.
topics.activity: Use a fictional before-and-after forest map to identify two possible effects and a question for local communities.

topics.name: Reading a migration flow map
topics.description: Flow maps use arrows to show the direction of movement; wider arrows may represent larger flows when explained by a key.
topics.locator: PDF p. 35, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Geography > Year 7 practices
objectives: Use a map key to compare the size of migration flows shown by arrows.
evidence: Uses the arrow direction and key to compare fictional migration flows.
misconceptions: Every arrow on a flow map necessarily represents the same number of people.
topics.question: On a flow map where wider arrows mean more people, what does a wider arrow indicate?
topics.answer: It indicates a larger flow of people along that route.
topics.explanation: The map's key explains how arrow width relates to the quantity of movement.
hints: Read the map key first.
The wider arrow stands for a larger number in this map.
topics.activity: Draw two fictional flows between places with different arrow widths and add a key explaining the quantities.

topics.name: The four Rs of emergency management
topics.description: Emergency management includes reduction, readiness, response and recovery, which address different stages of risk and its aftermath.
topics.locator: PDF p. 35, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Geography > Year 8 knowledge
objectives: Identify readiness as preparation before an emergency.
evidence: Identifies readiness as preparing before an emergency.
misconceptions: Recovery only means what people do before a hazard occurs.
topics.question: Which of the four Rs includes preparing a household emergency plan before a hazard?
topics.answer: Readiness.
topics.explanation: Readiness involves preparing in advance; response and recovery address immediate and longer-term needs after an event.
hints: Think about the stage before an emergency.
Preparing is readiness.
topics.activity: Match fictional examples of reducing risk, preparing, responding and rebuilding to the four Rs; check current local guidance with an adult.

topics.name: China and the Treaty of Nanjing
topics.description: After the First Opium War, the 1842 Treaty of Nanjing required China to open additional ports and cede Hong Kong Island.
topics.locator: PDF p. 33, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > History > Year 7 alternative case study
objectives: Identify a consequence of the Treaty of Nanjing following the First Opium War.
evidence: Identifies a consequence of the treaty while recognising that it followed conflict.
misconceptions: The treaty was simply an equal trading agreement reached without conflict.
topics.question: What was one requirement imposed on China by the Treaty of Nanjing in 1842?
topics.answer: China had to open additional ports or cede Hong Kong Island.
topics.explanation: The treaty followed the First Opium War and imposed terms that expanded British access and control.
hints: Look for a change affecting ports or territory.
The treaty required additional ports to open.
topics.activity: Place the First Opium War and the Treaty of Nanjing on a timeline, then compare two sourced perspectives on their consequences.

topics.name: Silk Roads and exchanges
topics.description: The Silk Roads were networks along which goods, people, ideas and technologies moved across regions.
topics.locator: PDF p. 34, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > History > Year 7 alternative case study
objectives: Identify goods, people, ideas or technologies exchanged along the Silk Roads.
evidence: Identifies more than one type of exchange along trade networks.
misconceptions: Only silk ever travelled on the Silk Roads.
topics.question: What travelled along the Silk Roads besides goods such as silk?
topics.answer: People, ideas, religions and technologies also moved along these networks.
topics.explanation: Merchants and other travellers connected many places, carrying knowledge as well as goods.
hints: Think about the travellers as well as what they sold.
Ideas and technologies also moved.
topics.activity: On a simplified map, draw a trade route and add one good and one idea or technology that travelled between regions.

topics.name: Westward expansion and Indigenous peoples
topics.description: United States westward expansion displaced many Native American peoples and disrupted access to land and resources.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 33–34, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > History > Year 8 alternative case study
objectives: Identify a consequence of westward expansion for Native American communities.
evidence: Identifies an effect of expansion on Indigenous peoples while recognising their continuing agency.
misconceptions: Native American peoples simply disappeared as settlers expanded west.
topics.question: What was one consequence of westward expansion for many Native American communities?
topics.answer: Many faced loss of land, forced displacement or disruption of access to resources.
topics.explanation: Expansion and broken or imposed treaties affected Indigenous communities, who also resisted and continue to maintain and renew their cultures.
hints: Consider what happened to land and movement.
Loss of land or forced displacement is one consequence.
topics.activity: Compare an Indigenous account with another historical source about a specific event, identifying whose voices are represented.

topics.name: Partition and independence in South Asia
topics.description: In 1947 British India was partitioned as India and Pakistan became independent, followed by mass migration and violence.
topics.locator: PDF p. 46, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > History > Year 9 alternative case study
objectives: Describe migration or displacement associated with the 1947 partition of British India.
evidence: Explains that independence was accompanied by displacement and conflict.
misconceptions: The achievement of independence meant that no communities experienced loss or displacement.
topics.question: What happened to many people during the 1947 partition of British India?
topics.answer: Many crossed new borders or were displaced, and violence affected communities.
topics.explanation: Independence and partition changed political boundaries and caused large movements of people and significant loss of life.
hints: Think about the new borders and the people living on either side.
Many people migrated or were forced from their homes.
topics.activity: Use a teacher-selected historical map to compare the borders before and after 1947 and ask whose experiences a source records.

topics.name: Tonga and the British protectorate
topics.description: Tonga was a British protected state from 1900 to 1970 while retaining its Indigenous monarchy and self-government.
topics.locator: PDF p. 45, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > History > Year 9 alternative case study
objectives: Recognise that Tonga retained its Indigenous monarchy during the British protectorate.
evidence: Distinguishes a period of protectorate status from the end of self-government.
misconceptions: Tonga's monarchy and self-government ceased throughout the protectorate.
topics.question: Did Tonga retain its Indigenous monarchy during the British protectorate?
topics.answer: Yes. Tonga retained its monarchy and self-government while it was a British protected state.
topics.explanation: The protectorate affected external relationships, but Tonga continued to have its own monarchy and government.
hints: Consider the status of the monarchy during 1900–1970.
The monarchy continued.
topics.activity: Make a timeline of the protectorate and its end using a Tongan or other reliable historical source.

topics.name: New Zealand in the Second World War
topics.description: New Zealand's Second World War participation included military service and work on the home front, including service by the 28th Māori Battalion.
topics.locator: PDF p. 43, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > History > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Identify a home-front contribution to New Zealand's Second World War effort.
evidence: Identifies a military and a home-front contribution.
misconceptions: Only people serving overseas contributed to the Second World War effort.
topics.question: Besides overseas military service, what was one way people in New Zealand contributed during the Second World War?
topics.answer: People worked or volunteered on the home front, including in essential production and services.
topics.explanation: War affected communities as well as military personnel, with different groups contributing in different ways.
hints: Think about workplaces and support at home.
Essential work and volunteering were contributions.
topics.activity: Compare a sourced account of the 28th Māori Battalion with a home-front account and identify each person's contribution.

topics.name: Different community observances
topics.description: Communities may mark cultural, faith or national occasions in different ways, and people may choose different ways to take part.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9, Phase 1 (Years 0–3) > Civics and Society > Year 2 knowledge
objectives: Suggest a respectful way to learn what an observance means to someone.
evidence: Describes one respectful way to learn about an observance without assuming everyone celebrates it.
misconceptions: Every person in a community observes the same occasion in the same way.
topics.question: How can you learn what an occasion means to someone without assuming their experience?
topics.answer: Ask respectfully or use a source the community has chosen to share.
topics.explanation: People's traditions and personal choices vary, even within the same community.
hints: Think about listening to the people concerned.
Ask rather than assuming.
topics.activity: Compare two fictional invitations and list one respectful question about how each event is observed.

topics.name: Hīnaki and food gathering
topics.description: Māori developed technologies such as hīnaki, woven traps used to gather tuna, using materials and knowledge suited to their context.
topics.locator: PDF p. 10, Phase 1 (Years 0–3) > History > Year 3 knowledge; additional example or community evidence linked in activity resources
objectives: Identify the food-gathering purpose of a hīnaki without inventing local practices.
evidence: Identifies the food-gathering purpose of a hīnaki without inventing local practices.
misconceptions: People in the past gathered all food without designing or making tools.
topics.question: What is a hīnaki used for in the food-gathering examples studied here?
topics.answer: It is a woven trap used to gather tuna.
topics.explanation: Its design is an example of technology developed for obtaining food; specific practices and knowledge belong to the communities concerned.
hints: The tool is associated with gathering tuna.
It is a woven trap.
topics.activity: Study a teacher-selected, appropriately shared image of a hīnaki and describe its visible form and stated use without making claims about local tikanga.

resources.label: Te Papa: Hīnaki (eel trap)
resources.attribution: Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa; image rights remain reserved.

topics.name: Moriori covenant of peace
topics.description: Moriori histories describe an ancestral covenant of peace that renounced warfare and killing; Nunuku was among the karāpuna who reaffirmed it on Rēkohu.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 19–20, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > History > Year 4 knowledge; Hokotehi Moriori Trust Deed p. 4, Covenant of Peace, linked in activity resources
objectives: Identify peace as a principle of the ancestral Moriori covenant reaffirmed by Nunuku, and recognise Moriori as a living people.
evidence: Identifies peace as a principle of the ancestral Moriori covenant reaffirmed by Nunuku and recognises Moriori as a living people.
misconceptions: Moriori history and identity ended in the past.
topics.question: According to Moriori histories, what principle did Nunuku reaffirm in the ancestral covenant of peace?
topics.answer: A commitment to peace and the renunciation of warfare.
topics.explanation: Hokotehi Moriori Trust describes the covenant as handed down from earlier ancestors and reaffirmed by Nunuku and other karāpuna. Moriori culture and identity continue today.
hints: Think about the value handed down by earlier ancestors.
It affirmed peace and renounced warfare.
topics.activity: With a teacher, read an age-appropriate extract from the publicly shared Hokotehi Moriori Trust account or deed, then write one question about how the community preserves its history.

resources.label: Hokotehi Moriori Trust: Our Story
resources.attribution: Hokotehi Moriori Trust; use community materials with respect.

resources.label: Hokotehi Moriori Trust Deed: Covenant of Peace, p. 4
resources.attribution: Hokotehi Moriori Trust; teachers should select age-appropriate extracts and respect community source terms.

topics.name: Meri Te Tai Mangakāhia and representation
topics.description: In 1893 Meri Te Tai Mangakāhia of Te Rarawa advocated for women to vote and stand in the Kotahitanga Māori Parliament.
topics.locator: PDF p. 19, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > History > Year 6 knowledge; additional example or community evidence linked in activity resources
objectives: Identify the participation Meri Te Tai Mangakāhia advocated in the Kotahitanga Māori Parliament.
evidence: Identifies the specific parliament and the participation she advocated.
misconceptions: Women won the right to stand in New Zealand's national Parliament at the same time as they gained the vote in 1893.
topics.question: What change did Meri Te Tai Mangakāhia advocate in the Kotahitanga Māori Parliament?
topics.answer: She sought women's right to vote for members and to stand as members of that parliament.
topics.explanation: Her advocacy addressed representation in the Kotahitanga Parliament; voting rights and eligibility for different parliaments followed distinct histories.
hints: Which parliament was she addressing?
She argued for women's voting and representation in the Kotahitanga Parliament.
topics.activity: Use the linked NZ History biography to make a two-event timeline of her 1893 advocacy and a question about representation.

resources.label: NZ History: Meri Mangakāhia
resources.attribution: Manatū Taonga – Ministry for Culture and Heritage; see source terms.

topics.name: The two treaty texts
topics.description: Te Tiriti o Waitangi and the English Treaty of Waitangi have different wording; most rangatira signed the te reo Māori text.
topics.locator: PDF p. 32, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > History > Year 8 knowledge; additional example or community evidence linked in activity resources
objectives: Identify the te reo Māori treaty text as the version signed by most rangatira.
evidence: Identifies the text most rangatira signed and recognises that interpretation requires careful source comparison.
misconceptions: The two 1840 texts use identical wording and have never been interpreted differently.
topics.question: Which text did most rangatira sign in 1840?
topics.answer: Most signed the te reo Māori text, Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
topics.explanation: The Māori and English texts use different language, and their meanings and consequences continue to be discussed and interpreted.
hints: The two texts were written in different languages.
Most signed the te reo Māori text.
topics.activity: Use the linked Waitangi Tribunal resource to compare the names of the two texts and list a question about interpretation; do not assume all rangatira held one view.

topics.name: Land confiscation and communities
topics.description: Following conflicts in the New Zealand Wars, Crown confiscation of Māori land caused deep losses for affected communities.
topics.locator: PDF p. 42, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > History > Year 9 knowledge; additional example or community evidence linked in activity resources
objectives: Identify land loss as a consequence of Crown confiscation for affected Māori communities.
evidence: Identifies land loss as a consequence while recognising that impacts differed across communities.
misconceptions: Land confiscation had no continuing effects on Māori communities.
topics.question: What was one consequence of Crown land confiscations after the New Zealand Wars?
topics.answer: Affected Māori communities lost land, with consequences for their relationships, resources and authority.
topics.explanation: Raupatu affected whenua and the people connected to it; the effects and historical experiences vary across places and communities.
hints: Think about the land held by affected whānau and hapū.
The confiscation caused loss of whenua.
topics.activity: Use a published iwi, hapū or Waitangi Tribunal account to identify one consequence and one question requiring local evidence.
materials: publicly shared community or Tribunal source

resources.label: NZ History: the Waikato-Tainui claim
resources.attribution: Manatū Taonga – Ministry for Culture and Heritage; this is one regional example.

topics.name: Pacific service in the First World War
topics.description: Pacific Islanders, including people from the Cook Islands and Niue, served with New Zealand forces during the First World War.
topics.locator: PDF p. 42, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > History > Year 10 knowledge; additional example or community evidence linked in activity resources
objectives: Name a Pacific community whose members served with New Zealand forces in the First World War.
evidence: Names one Pacific community whose members served and avoids treating all experiences as identical.
misconceptions: Only people born in New Zealand served with New Zealand forces in the First World War.
topics.question: Name one Pacific community whose members served with New Zealand forces in the First World War.
topics.answer: People from the Cook Islands or Niue are examples.
topics.explanation: People from several Pacific communities contributed to the war effort, with different individual experiences.
hints: Think about Pacific islands named in the curriculum.
The Cook Islands and Niue are examples.
topics.activity: Use a teacher-selected historical source to identify one Pacific service contribution and one question about an individual's experience.

topics.name: Recording daily weather
topics.description: Geographers can observe and record weather such as rainfall, cloud cover and temperature over a short period.
topics.locator: PDF p. 13, Phase 1 (Years 0–3) > Geography > Year 2 practices
objectives: Distinguish a one-day weather observation from a long-term climate pattern.
evidence: Records an observation as a specific day rather than claiming it describes a long-term climate.
misconceptions: One rainy day proves what a place's climate is always like.
topics.question: A learner records rain on Monday. What does that observation describe?
topics.answer: It describes the weather observed on that day.
topics.explanation: A short observation records conditions at a particular time; a long-term climate pattern needs many observations over a longer period.
hints: Think about the time covered by one observation.
One day describes that day's weather.
topics.activity: Make a three-day fictional weather table and describe one change without claiming it represents a long-term climate.

topics.name: Using a map scale for distance
topics.description: A map scale relates a distance on the map to a distance in the represented place.
topics.locator: PDF p. 25, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Geography > Year 4 knowledge
objectives: Calculate map distance from a stated fictional scale.
evidence: Calculates a simple distance from a stated fictional scale.
misconceptions: One centimetre on every map represents the same real-world distance.
topics.question: On a fictional map, 1 cm represents 5 km. What distance does a 2 cm line represent?
topics.answer: It represents 10 km.
topics.explanation: Two map centimetres each stand for 5 km, so 2 × 5 = 10 km.
hints: What does each centimetre represent?
Multiply 2 by 5 km.
topics.activity: Draw a fictional 1 cm to 5 km scale and label the distance represented by 3 cm.

topics.name: Māori migration to cities
topics.description: After the Second World War, many Māori moved from rural areas to cities for opportunities, while maintaining and creating connections in different ways.
topics.locator: PDF p. 36, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Geography > Year 7 knowledge; additional example or community evidence linked in activity resources
objectives: Identify one reason many Māori moved to cities after the Second World War.
evidence: Explains one reason for migration and recognises varied experiences and continuing connections.
misconceptions: All Māori people who moved to cities lost every connection to their communities.
topics.question: What was one reason many Māori moved to cities after the Second World War?
topics.answer: Some moved for employment and other opportunities.
topics.explanation: Migration decisions varied, and people maintained or created community connections in different ways.
hints: Think about opportunities available in cities.
Employment was one reason.
topics.activity: Use the linked Māori-authored Te Ara account to identify one opportunity and one continuing or new connection; do not ask classmates to disclose family histories.

resources.label: Te Ara: Urban Māori, by Paul Meredith
resources.attribution: Paul Meredith, Te Ara – Manatū Taonga; see source terms.

topics.name: Urban surfaces and flood risk
topics.description: Concrete and other impermeable surfaces reduce the amount of rain that soaks into the ground and can increase surface runoff.
topics.locator: PDF p. 36, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Geography > Year 8 knowledge
objectives: Explain how impermeable urban surfaces can increase runoff during heavy rain.
evidence: Explains how a surface that absorbs less water can affect runoff.
misconceptions: Water soaks into concrete in the same way as into permeable soil.
topics.question: Why can a large paved area contribute to surface flooding during heavy rain?
topics.answer: Less water can soak into the ground, so more may flow across the surface.
topics.explanation: Impermeable surfaces change where rainwater goes; drainage, slope and rainfall also influence local flood risk.
hints: Compare what happens to rain on soil and pavement.
More water remains on the surface of pavement.
topics.activity: Draw arrows on two fictional catchment diagrams, one mostly soil and one mostly pavement, showing possible runoff; stay away from floodwater.

topics.name: The 2011 Christchurch earthquake
topics.description: The February 2011 Christchurch earthquake caused severe shaking and liquefaction that damaged buildings and infrastructure.
topics.locator: PDF p. 36, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Geography > Year 8 knowledge; teacher-selected illustrative case; specific event supported by linked public source, not named in the curriculum text
objectives: Identify an infrastructure effect of liquefaction in the 2011 Christchurch earthquake.
evidence: Identifies an infrastructure effect supported by the linked public historical account.
misconceptions: An earthquake can affect buildings but not roads or underground services.
topics.question: What infrastructure was damaged by liquefaction during the 2011 Christchurch earthquake?
topics.answer: Roads and underground services such as water and sewer pipes were damaged.
topics.explanation: Shaking and liquefaction affected multiple parts of the city; impacts varied by place and by people's circumstances.
hints: Think about services below streets as well as the roads.
Water and sewer pipes were among the damaged infrastructure.
topics.activity: Use a teacher-selected extract from the linked NZ History account to list one physical effect and one effect on daily life; learners need not share personal experiences.

resources.label: NZ History: February 2011 Christchurch earthquake
resources.attribution: Manatū Taonga – Ministry for Culture and Heritage; teachers may select age-appropriate excerpts.

topics.name: Cyclone Gabrielle and connected hazards
topics.description: Cyclone Gabrielle in February 2023 caused severe flooding and landslides in parts of the eastern North Island, including Hawke's Bay.
topics.locator: PDF p. 35, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Geography > Year 8 knowledge; teacher-selected illustrative case; specific event supported by linked public source, not named in the curriculum text
objectives: Identify flooding and landslides as connected impacts of Cyclone Gabrielle in Hawke's Bay.
evidence: Identifies flooding and landslides as connected impacts in a documented event.
misconceptions: A severe storm can cause only one kind of environmental impact.
topics.question: What hazard occurred alongside flooding during Cyclone Gabrielle in parts of Hawke's Bay?
topics.answer: Landslides occurred, carrying soil and sediment into affected areas.
topics.explanation: Intense rain contributed to several connected processes, with impacts varying across places and communities.
hints: Think about what can happen on steep land during intense rain.
Landslides were another major hazard.
topics.activity: Use the linked Earth Sciences New Zealand research summary to draw a cause-and-effect chain from intense rain to landslides, sediment and an impact on a place; avoid entering hazardous areas.
materials: linked Earth Sciences New Zealand research summary
