topics.name: Longshore drift
topics.description: Waves arriving at an angle can move sediment along a coastline through a process called longshore drift.
topics.locator: PDF p. 49, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Geography > Year 9 knowledge
objectives: Describe how waves can move sediment along a coastline.
evidence: Distinguishes movement of sediment along the coast from deposition in one place.
misconceptions: Waves can transport beach sediment only straight out to sea.
topics.question: What is longshore drift?
topics.answer: It is the movement of sediment along a coast as waves approach and return.
topics.explanation: Wave direction and repeated movement of water can transfer sediment along the shore, where it may later be deposited.
hints: Does the material move along or across the coast?
Longshore drift moves it along the coast.
topics.activity: Draw an angled wave, the shoreline and an arrow showing sediment moving along the coast.

topics.name: Emergency and development aid
topics.description: Emergency aid responds to immediate needs, while development aid supports longer-term goals; programmes can overlap.
topics.locator: PDF p. 50, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Geography > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Distinguish immediate emergency aid from a longer-term development project.
evidence: Distinguishes an immediate emergency response from a longer-term project in a fictional example.
misconceptions: All aid programmes have exactly the same time frame and purpose.
topics.question: Which is an example of emergency aid: supplying safe water after a flood or building a school over several years?
topics.answer: Supplying safe water immediately after a flood is emergency aid.
topics.explanation: The first response addresses an urgent need; the school project is a longer-term example.
hints: Which need is immediate?
Safe water after a flood is an urgent response.
topics.activity: Sort fictional aid examples by their immediate or longer-term purpose and explain where a project might serve both.

topics.name: Exchange fees and a budget
topics.description: An exchange provider may charge a fee, so a budget should consider both the rate and the stated fee.
topics.locator: PDF p. 37, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Financial and Economic Activity > Year 7 knowledge
objectives: Calculate a fictional currency amount after a fee in the same units.
evidence: Calculates a fictional amount after a fee charged in the same currency.
misconceptions: The exchange rate is the only factor that can affect how much currency is received.
topics.question: A fictional exchange yields 20 units before a fee of 2 units. How many units remain after that fee?
topics.answer: 18 units remain.
topics.explanation: The stated fee is subtracted from the amount received: 20 − 2 = 18 units.
hints: Both amounts use the same fictional units.
Subtract the fee from 20.
topics.activity: Compare two fictional exchange offers with stated rates and fees, ensuring all amounts use compatible units.

topics.name: Income and costs in an event budget
topics.description: A group can compare expected income with all estimated costs when planning an event.
topics.locator: PDF p. 37, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Financial and Economic Activity > Year 7 practices
objectives: Calculate the amount left after estimated costs are subtracted from fictional event income.
evidence: Calculates the surplus in a simple fictional event budget.
misconceptions: A group can judge an event budget from income without considering costs.
topics.question: A fictional event expects $60 income and $35 total costs. What amount remains if both estimates are met?
topics.answer: $25 remains.
topics.explanation: Subtract estimated costs from estimated income: $60 − $35 = $25; actual results may differ.
hints: What is the total cost?
Subtract $35 from $60.
topics.activity: Build a fictional event budget including one source of income and two itemised costs, then check whether it stays within the estimate.

topics.name: Debit and credit payments
topics.description: Debit payments generally use funds available in an account, while credit uses a borrowing facility that must be repaid under its terms.
topics.locator: PDF p. 37, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Financial and Economic Activity > Year 8 knowledge
objectives: Distinguish payment from available account funds from credit that must be repaid.
evidence: Distinguishes using available account funds from using borrowed money.
misconceptions: A credit card always uses only money already in the holder's bank account.
topics.question: Which payment method generally involves borrowing to be repaid later: debit or credit?
topics.answer: Credit generally uses borrowed funds that must be repaid.
topics.explanation: Debit generally draws on available account funds, while credit creates an obligation; actual account and card terms can vary.
hints: Which method creates a borrowing obligation?
Credit involves borrowing.
topics.activity: Sort fictional payment scenarios into using available account funds and borrowing, without using real accounts or cards.

topics.name: Comparing insurance information
topics.description: Insurance information can describe risks covered, costs and exclusions; evaluating a policy requires reading its actual terms.
topics.locator: PDF p. 51, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Financial and Economic Activity > Year 9 practices
objectives: Identify coverage, exclusions and conditions to compare in fictional insurance summaries.
evidence: Identifies one coverage question and one cost to check in fictional policy information.
misconceptions: Buying any insurance automatically covers every loss without conditions.
topics.question: What should someone compare besides the price of two fictional insurance policies?
topics.answer: Compare what each covers, its exclusions and any stated excess or conditions.
topics.explanation: Policies can differ in both cost and coverage, so price alone cannot establish which one meets a person's circumstances.
hints: What might the policy not cover?
Check coverage, exclusions and conditions.
topics.activity: Compare two fictional policy summaries for a toy bicycle and identify a covered event, an exclusion and a stated cost; do not purchase insurance.

topics.name: Income and spending taxes
topics.description: Government collects taxes in different ways, including PAYE on employment income and GST on spending.
topics.locator: PDF p. 51, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Financial and Economic Activity > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Distinguish PAYE on employment income from GST on spending.
evidence: Distinguishes a tax associated with employment income from one associated with spending.
misconceptions: PAYE and GST are both simply names for the same kind of transaction.
topics.question: Which tax collection method is associated with employment income: PAYE or GST?
topics.answer: PAYE is associated with employment income.
topics.explanation: PAYE is deducted from employment income, while GST is generally a tax on goods and services; specific circumstances and rules vary.
hints: Think about wages rather than a shop purchase.
PAYE is associated with employment income.
topics.activity: Label two fictional examples, wages and a shop purchase, with the relevant tax type; do not use real payslips.

topics.name: Access, fees and savings decisions
topics.description: Savings options can differ in fees, interest and when money may be withdrawn, so a choice depends partly on when it is needed.
topics.locator: PDF p. 52, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Financial and Economic Activity > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Explain why withdrawal conditions matter for a short-term savings goal.
evidence: Identifies a withdrawal condition that matters for a stated short-term goal.
misconceptions: A higher advertised return always makes an account suitable regardless of withdrawal restrictions.
topics.question: A fictional goal needs money next month. Why check an account's withdrawal conditions?
topics.answer: The money may be difficult to access in time or an early withdrawal may have conditions or costs.
topics.explanation: The timing of a goal matters alongside fees and interest; the product's actual terms determine access.
hints: When is the money needed?
Check whether it can be withdrawn by then.
topics.activity: Compare two fictional accounts on withdrawal access, fees and interest for a stated goal; make no real financial decision.

topics.name: Checking financial advice
topics.description: Financial advice and tools can help with decisions, but users should check whether information is relevant, transparent about costs and potential conflicts, and suitable for their circumstances.
topics.locator: PDF p. 52, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Financial and Economic Activity > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Ask about fees, payments or conflicts when assessing financial advice.
evidence: Identifies a question about fees or conflicts to ask when assessing fictional advice.
misconceptions: Advice must be impartial simply because the person giving it sounds confident.
topics.question: What is one useful question to ask when assessing a financial recommendation?
topics.answer: Ask how the adviser is paid or what fees and conflicts may affect the recommendation.
topics.explanation: Understanding incentives and costs helps someone judge the information alongside their needs and other trustworthy sources.
hints: Could the person recommending a product benefit from the choice?
Ask about payment, fees or conflicts.
topics.activity: Compare two fictional advice disclosures and list what additional information each provides or omits; avoid using real financial details.
